newsitem.title: UK: Budget to dampen lively British housing market.
newsitem.headline: Budget to dampen lively British housing market.

text.p: A cut in mortgage interest tax relief (MIRAS) and expectations of higher interest rates after Wednesday's budget could quickly dampen activity in Britain's bubbling housing market, but the measures will hit the most depressed areas hardest.

Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown cut mortgage interest tax relief to 10 percent from 15 percent -- the tougher of two measures intended to slow activity in the housing market, and a move which will affect most of Britain's 10 million mortgage holders.

"But this will hit lower-income homeowners very hard and have the greatest impact on the market in the north of England and Scotland which is already less buoyant," said Alan Oliver, spokesman for the Nationwide Building Society.

Nationwide figures show house prices have soared 21 percent in the last year in London and are rising fast in the metropolitan areas just outside the capital and in the south east of England. But prices in the north of England have barely budged in the last year, and Scottish houses have actually slipped slightly lower.
Helen Dunn, an economist at Halifax Plc, Britain's biggest mortgage lender, said if the intention was to quell activity in the most buoyant areas, reducing MIRAS was not the right way to go about it.
"If the worry is that the market in London and the south east is overheating, the cut in MIRAS is not targeting the right area. It unduly punishes the more depressed north," she said.
The bank will be reviewing forecasts for house price rises this year next month. Halifax currently forecasts house prices rising by 7.0 this year, slowing to a 6.0 rise next.
MIRAS, a tax break on interest payments on the first 30,000 pounds of a home loan, benefits owners of cheaper housing most.
But the other measure directed at housing, a higher rate of stamp duty on property transactions, is likely to have little impact on the market.
Brown raised stamp duty to 1.5 percent from 1.0 percent on property purchases above 250,000 pounds, and to 2.0 percent on property purchases over 500,000 pounds.
"This will affect only around two percent of the market. It is a high yielder for the Treasury, but will have little success slowing the market down," said Dunn.
Andrew Dilnot, director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies, agreed.
"It is difficult to see how this rise in stamp duty would take any heat out of the housing market."
He said that in 1986, when the housing market was similarly buoyant, of the 822,000 properties bought and sold only 15,000 would have been affected by the new measures.
But higher interest rates could slow the market down by much more than these targeted measures combined.
Since tax rises aimed at the personal sector were in total only modest, financial markets assume monetary policy will now be largely responsible for demand management.
They are discounting a series of sharp interest rate rises which will hit the millions of home owners with floating rate mortgages.
Oliver said the Nationwide was considering revising its interest rate forecast in light of the budget.
"We are having a look at it. We have forecast rates at 7.0 percent by the end of the year. If they go higher than that it will certainly have a bearing on the housing market."
Helen Dunn of Halifax said its interest rates forecast may also be revised.

"Our interest rate forecast is for rates to peak at 7.5 percent next year," she said. "We probably won't change the peak, but the risk is that the rate rises all come sooner. The Bank of England is likely to be concerned at the little amount of tightening aimed at the personal sector."
Both mortgage lenders said they will be lobbying the government to replace MIRAS with a housing benefit for home owners on low incomes.
They will be joined by the homeless charity Shelter. It actually welcomed the cut in MIRAS, as long as it is replaced by a more carefully targeted benefit.
"The cut in MIRAS is to be welcomed. It is an untargeted subsidy paid to millionaires and paupers alike," said Shelter spokeswoman Susan Littlemore.
"Realistically, it does need to be reduced, but it should be replaced by a mortgage benefit scheme. The government must do something to help home owners at the margin."
Dunn said the government might well be sympathetic, but she does not expect any quick decision.

"The Labour party has been interested in ideas of those sort in the past. I think they know there is a gap there that the private sector cannot fill. But it may take the government some time to assess it."
